newsitem.title: UK: British trade union bank to branch into retail.
newsitem.headline: British trade union bank to branch into retail.

text.p: Britain's trade union owned Unity Trust Bank will pilot its first retail-targeted products during 1997, its managing director Gordon Beesley said on Tuesday.
"We are looking to move into the personal sector for the first time later this year," Beesley told a press briefing following the announcement of a 137 percent improvement in pretax profits for 1996.
Group pretax profit at the small bank, which was founded in 1984 and is 64 percent owned by British trades unions, rose to 1.283 million pounds ($2.1 million) from 541,000 pounds in 1995.
Britain's Co-operative Bank, itself a subsidiary of the Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS), owns 35.9 percent of Unity and a tiny portion is held by a number of individuals.

Beesley said Unity, which has no retail outlets, planned to develop "affinity based products" which would begin as deposit based. The move reflected an increasing shift in British banking towards plastic cards and remote banking, he said.

Unity's chairman Sir Dennis Landau said that while the group profit was relatively small, it represented an important stage in the bank's development. "We now know that we have got a good sound basis on which to build," he said.
While the bank may not match the percentage growth in future years, Beesley said he would be disappointed if it did not continue to grow.
Pre-tax profit at the bank itself rose by 10 percent to 729,000 stg and interest income rose by nearly 10 percent "thanks to a steady increase in current account balances".

Beesley said Unity had grown its customer base in the so-called "social economy" -- including charities, co-operatives and other voluntary sector organisations -- with retail deposits from this market now accounting for 30 percent of its total.
Unity could, he said, meet the growing demand for working capital and cashflow demands of such bodies, which were playing an increasingly important role in many areas of British society.
The bank said it would pay a dividend of one penny per ordinary share. It has only once paid a dividend in the past, in the mid 1980s.

Landau said that Unity's associated companies continued to eliminate their losses, which in earlier years had been due to start up costs while the bank itself now offered an increasing range of services.
Unity's share of losses from financial services company Unity Financial Holdings, which it owns jointly with Colonial Group, fell to 106,000 stg in 1996 from 549,000 stg a year before.
Jacques Martin Unity, which is developing industry-wide pension schemes and providing independent pensions consultancy for trades unions, reduced its losses to 216,000 stg from 248,000 stg.
And Unity Investment Management increased its fee income by 13 percent to 516,000 stg and funds under management rose to 159.6 million stg by the end of 1996 from 136.2 million stg at the start.
Landau, formerly chief executive of the Co-operative Wholesale Society, took the opportunity to voice his concerns about British pensions provision and the inadequacy of proposed changes.
"The proposals put forward by the Conservatives and Labour are no more than a step in the right direction. We believe that to tackle the problem there is a case for compulsory contributions."

Neither party, he said, was brave enough to call for compulsory contributions if it won the election on May 1 but such a move, which would make it mandatory for employers to contribute to a worker's second pension had to be made within two years.
Such an occupational or private pension would be in addition to the existing state pension which had to be maintained, he added.

"The present situation is grim," he said, adding that a top class debate was needed to address the problem that by 2030 pensions would be worth less than 10 percent of average earnings. ($ = 0.614 British Pounds)
